card.name: The Chicken
card.tagline: The 1950s R&B novelty step that evolved from a Twist variation to a funky 1970s anthem.
card.profile: The Chicken is an American rhythm and blues novelty dance that emerged in the 1950s, characterized by mimetic movements of a bird. Dancers mimic a chicken by flapping their arms and kicking their feet backward while maintaining a lateral body motion. Originally used as a rhythmic variation for the Twist, it achieved global recognition in 1970 through Rufus Thomas's 'Do the Funky Chicken' and later influenced Bob Fosse's choreography.
card.insight: Before Rufus Thomas made it a 1970s hit, the Chicken was a lateral 'change of pace' step used by dancers in the 1950s to break the rotation of the Twist.
card.profile_long:
The Chicken originated in the United States during the 1950s as a rhythmic expression within the rhythm and blues scene. In its earliest form, it served as a 'change of pace' step for dancers performing the Twist, allowing for a break in the repetitive swiveling motion with a more lateral, mimetic movement. The dance is defined by its literal interpretation of its namesake, requiring the dancer to flap their arms in imitation of wings and kick their feet back to mimic a bird's scratching or walking motion. This playful, novelty approach to social dancing reflected the era's interest in animal-themed steps and rhythmic experimentation.

By the 1960s, the physical vocabulary of the Chicken began to influence professional choreography and other social dance crazes. Most notably, the dance is cited as a precursor to the Frug, a popular 1960s dance that was famously showcased in the work of choreographer Bob Fosse. The transition from a simple R&B social step to a choreographed stage element highlights the dance's versatility and its role in the evolution of American vernacular movement. The lateral body movements and specific arm-flapping gestures provided a foundation for the more stylized, hip-heavy movements seen in the Frug.

In 1970, the dance underwent a major revival and transformation with the release of Rufus Thomas's hit record 'Do the Funky Chicken'. This version, often referred to as the 'Funky Chicken', brought the 1950s step into the funk era, emphasizing a more syncopated and energetic execution. The song became a staple of the Stax Records sound and solidified the dance's place in pop culture history. The performance of the dance by Thomas, often involving comedic interaction with the audience, reinforced its status as a communal, high-energy novelty dance that bridged the gap between R&B and early funk.

The Chicken's cultural footprint extended into the late 20th century through various media appearances. It was featured in the 1980 film 'The Blues Brothers', directed by John Landis, where it served as a visual marker of the R&B and soul tradition the film celebrated. Furthermore, the dance was immortalized in the 1997 Chicago Tribune column by Mary Schmich, 'Advice, like youth, probably just wasted on the young', which was later adapted into the 1999 hit song 'Wear Sunscreen' by Baz Luhrmann. These references ensure that while the dance may no longer be a primary club staple, its movements remain a recognizable part of the American dance lexicon.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance emerged in the United States during the 1950s within the rhythm and blues community. It was initially a novelty step used to vary the movement of the Twist. It gained significant commercial traction in 1970 following the release of the song 'Do the Funky Chicken' by Rufus Thomas.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Dancers perform lateral body movements while flapping their arms to imitate a chicken's wings. Simultaneously, the feet are kicked back in a rhythmic fashion. It was traditionally used as a change-of-pace step during other dances like the Twist.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance is primarily performed to rhythm and blues and funk music. Key instruments include the electric guitar, bass, drums, and brass sections typical of the Stax Records sound. The most iconic musical accompaniment is Rufus Thomas's 1970 hit.
sections.costume_and_setting: There is no specific traditional costume, as it is a social novelty dance. It was typically performed in dance halls, clubs, and on televised music programs like Soul Train during its 1970s peak.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The Chicken is a secular social dance intended for entertainment and rhythmic expression. It serves as a lighthearted 'novelty' dance, often used to engage a crowd or provide a rhythmic break in a longer dance set.
sections.notable_figures: Rufus Thomas is the most significant figure associated with the dance's 1970s revival. Bob Fosse is noted for incorporating elements of the Chicken into the Frug. John Belushi and Dan Aykroyd performed it in 'The Blues Brothers'.
sections.regional_variants: While originating in the US R&B scene, the 'Funky Chicken' variant of 1970 is the most distinct evolution, adding funk-era syncopation to the original 1950s R&B step.
sections.lineage: The Chicken is a subclass of novelty dance. It gave rise to the Frug in the 1960s and is closely linked to the evolution of the Twist and the development of funk dance styles.

basic_steps: Flap both arms at the elbows in imitation of wings
Kick one foot back toward the glutes
Alternate feet while maintaining lateral body movement
Incorporate a slight forward lean of the torso
teaching.rhythm: 4/4 time, typically following a steady R&B or funk backbeat
teaching.level_notes: Beginners should focus on the arm flapping and foot-kicking coordination before adding the lateral body sway.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Strong backbeat on 2 and 4 with syncopated bass lines
music_profile.vocal_style: Soulful, rhythmic, often including call-and-response or spoken instructions
music_profile.sound_description: A driving funk or R&B sound characterized by a prominent brass section, a syncopated 'popping' bass line, and a steady drum beat that encourages repetitive, rhythmic movement.

movement_profile.posture: Slightly crouched or forward-leaning torso to facilitate the bird-like aesthetic.
movement_profile.footwork: Rhythmic backward kicks of the feet, alternating left and right, often described as 'kicking back their feet'.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Arms are bent at the elbows and flapped up and down at the sides like wings.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Lateral (side-to-side) body movements are integrated with the arm and leg motions.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Usually performed in place (stationary) or with minor lateral travel; solo social dance.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Bouncy and syncopated, matching the 'funky' rhythm of the music.

signature_moves.name: The Wing Flap
signature_moves.description: Bending elbows and moving them vertically to mimic a chicken's wings.

signature_moves.name: The Scratch Kick
signature_moves.description: Kicking the feet backward in time with the beat.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Low to medium levels; no significant jumps, primarily grounded stepping.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid overly stiff posture; the movement should be fluid and lateral rather than strictly vertical.

seniors.seated_version: Perform the arm flapping while seated; tap heels or lift knees slightly instead of kicking back to maintain balance.
seniors.standing_version: Hold onto a chair for balance while performing small backward foot taps; reduce the range of the arm flapping.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Perform at half-tempo; keep arm movements below shoulder height.
seniors.counts: Standard 1-2-3-4 counts, focusing on one limb at a time.
avoid: Full backward kicks that shift center of gravity

children.game_version: A 'Follow the Leader' style game where children must 'cluck' and flap whenever the music gets louder.
